title: A-Ch-D
hook: echad, one, as in the Shema

segments.voice: Yesterday, K-H-L: kahal, kehillah, the whole crowd gathered, the kids and the stranger too. Your line was community. Who did you gather? Today, the end of the week, and a word that holds it together. Day one thousand four hundred seven.

The first chapter of Genesis counts the days of creation. Day two, a second day. Day three, a third. But the first one isn't called the first. In the Hebrew, after the light and the dark and the evening and the morning, the verse says: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Not first. One. The commentator Rashi noticed it and gave a reason: on that day God was alone, the only one in the world. Ordinal numbers come later. On day one there is only one. Today's root is that word.
screen: `DAY TWO, DAY THREE...` → `BUT NOT THE FIRST DAY.` → `ONE DAY.`

segments.voice: A-Ch-D. Alef, chet, dalet. Echad: one. Turn it three ways. First, the Shema, the line said morning and night, and at the end of a life: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Echad is its last word. The Talmud says that whoever draws out the word echad when saying it, has their days drawn out. So the custom is to linger on it, especially on the last letter, and in that pause to let God's oneness fill everything: heaven, earth, and the four directions. Second, people. In Genesis, a couple becomes basar echad, one flesh. At Sinai, a teaching of the rabbis says the people camped facing the mountain like one person with one heart. Echad isn't only a number. It's the word for many becoming whole. Third, this week. It started with G-D-L, gadol, great, and growing. Then K-T-N, katan, the small one in the field. S-M-Ch, simcha, joy with a guest list. A-V-L, avel, the mourner, and friends who sat in silence. Sh-K-N, the presence that dwells with the neighbors. K-H-L, the crowd gathered to hear. Great and small, joy and grief, the neighbor and the crowd. They sound like opposites. Today's word holds them in one sentence. The same Shema is said on a wedding morning and in a shiva house, by the tallest and the smallest voice in the room. One isn't the opposite of many. One is what many can become.
screen: `THE LAST WORD OF THE SHEMA.` · `LINGER ON ECHAD.` · `ONE FLESH, ONE HEART.` · `THE WEEK: GREAT, SMALL, JOY, GRIEF, NEIGHBOR, CROWD.` · then, large: `ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing at a time. Settle, and breathe. For the length of the bell, choose one thing only. Just breathing. Or just listening to the room. Or just feeling your hands. When your mind starts a second thing, a list, a worry, a plan, notice it, and come back to the one. No scolding. Just back. If you pray, you can say the Shema slowly, and stay a while on the last word, the way the custom lingers on echad. If you don't, simply breathe out long on the word one. The bell holds the time.
screen: `CHOOSE ONE THING.` · `NOTICE THE SECOND.` · `COME BACK TO ONE.`

segments.voice: A-Ch-D. Alef, chet, dalet: the root of echad, one, the last word of the Shema, and the first day of creation. Today's word.
Your line: one. Today, pick one task, put the phone in another room, and do only that until it's done. Day one thousand four hundred seven.

howItsDone: Jews say the Shema morning and evening, traditionally covering the eyes for the first line and lingering on its last word, echad, with the intention that God is one.

fork.setup: you're writing Genesis 1. day two is 'a second day', day three 'a third day'. what do you call day one?
fork.reveal: the Hebrew says yom echad, one day. Rashi's reason: on that day there was only one, God alone.

original.note: Hebrew: one, the last word of the Shema, from the root alef, chet, dalet.

trapdoor: what you thought: echad is just the number one.
what it means: it's the Shema's last word, the one day of creation, and two becoming one flesh.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 13b on drawing out echad; Rashi on Genesis 1:5 explains yom echad, not yom rishon.

notes: Editor pass: 'a wedding week' changed to 'a wedding morning' (the Shema is said in every morning service); no other changes.
Genesis 1:5 and Deuteronomy 6:4 quoted as JPS 1917; confirm exact wording and punctuation.
Rashi on Genesis 1:5 paraphrased: Scripture says 'one day' rather than 'first day' because God was alone (yachid) in His world. Confirm.

Berakhot 13b paraphrased: whoever prolongs echad has his days and years prolonged; the custom to dwell on the dalet and intend God's kingship over heaven, earth and the four directions is from the same passage. Confirm.
Rashi on Exodus 19:2 ('like one man with one heart', from the Mekhilta) paraphrased as 'a teaching of the rabbis'. Confirm.
'Said morning and night, and at the end of a life' refers to the twice-daily recitation and the deathbed custom; confirm phrasing.
Week end (1401–1407): the teach looks back on G-D-L, K-T-N, S-M-Ch, A-V-L, Sh-K-N, K-H-L. Day 1401 was not yet on disk when this was written; its review link uses the index (gadol, great, to grow).
